newsitem.title: UK: Don't hurt housing market in UK budget - B/Society.
newsitem.headline: Don't hurt housing market in UK budget - B/Society.

text.p: A leading UK building society, Birmingham Midshires, urged Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Thursday not to hurt the housing market in his July 2 budget by removing tax breaks for mortgage holders.

"The abolition of MIRAS (mortgage interest relief at source), or increased property taxes, will be a kick in the teeth for the property market," said Mike Jackson, chief executive of Birmingham Midshires.
The housing market is currently showing steady signs of recovery and already has to deal with two official interest rate increases, which mean higher mortgage costs, in the last two months, he said.

"Removing MIRAS will have a detrimental impact on the number of first time buyers stepping on to the property ladder, because MIRAS accounts for a significant slice of their monthly mortgage payments," he said.
The society said MIRAS cost the government 2.7 billion stg in fiscal 1995-96.

Pressure is mounting on Chancellor Brown to do something to check burgeoning consumer demand, amid a surge in confidence following a spate of windfall payments from building society mergers or flotations.

Jackson warns that millions of lower income homeowners in the Midlands, North of England, Wales and Scotland, will suffer most in percentage terms if MIRAS is scrapped in the budget. Average home loans are smaller in these areas so the MIRAS benefit has a bigger impact on the monthly repayments.

The average mortgage in the North is 51,379 stg so abolishing MIRAS would increase mortgage costs there by 12 percent compared with an increase of just seven percent for those in the South East where the average mortgage is 86,558 stg, the building society said.

In a letter to the Chancellor, the society also warns that if Brown increases the level of stamp duty on property sales above its current ceiling of one percent on transactions above 60,000 stg, this would also increase homebuyers costs substantially.
